Voting

LogicCountingPermutations
Game: Groups of voters rank the same choices, and four different ways of counting can pick different winners. Find out who wins each time and whether the methods agree.
How to play: Type how many voters are in a column and click a name to move it up that ballot. Choose a method, then press its button to see the scores.
Candidates 3 Ballots 2
Look for the math

The four methods all use the same preference schedule: each column is a ballot, with the number of voters who cast it on top. Counting is easy; deciding what a fair count means is not. Here are the four rules the applet uses.

Counting first places, and counting every place

Plurality looks only at the top row: a candidate gets the voters whose ballot lists them first. The scores always add up to the number of voters. Borda count uses every place: with n candidates a first place is worth n points, the next n − 1, down to 1 for last. One ballot gives out n(n+1)/2 points in all. On the starting schedule, plurality elects A (5 to 4) but Borda elects B (22 to 19 to 13): counting the lower places changed the answer. The applet calls the final Borda list "first place votes" too; those numbers are Borda points.

Strike out the weakest, one round at a time

In plurality with elimination, each round every ballot gives its voters to the highest candidate still in the running. The weakest candidate is struck out and the round is counted again. When two are left, the one with more votes wins; equal votes give "Tied elections" and nobody wins. The applet's button then says "Restore", which walks back through the rounds. A candidate with more than half of all votes keeps them in every round and cannot be eliminated.

Head-to-head points

In pairwise comparison, every pair of candidates meets once. Whoever is higher on more ballots gets 1 point; a tie gives each .5 point. There are n(n−1)/2 meetings and exactly that many points to hand out. A candidate who beats every other candidate head to head, a Condorcet winner, always tops this count, but can still lose a plurality vote. Arrow's theorem explains why no simple rule can honour every fairness wish at once.

Checking the counts

The logic test scores all 19,152 schedules with three candidates, two or three ballots and up to six voters a second time, straight from the applet's bytecode: every first-place count, every (n − rank) × voters term, every head-to-head point and every elimination round agrees. Ties keep the applet's order, including the order of java.util.Hashtable keys when a weakest candidate must be chosen. The applet was made for Peter Tannenbaum's Excursions in Modern Mathematics and is reproduced with permission; its rules are used here, but this counting code is newly written.

Start with the 5-to-4 schedule, then move one B from the second ballot to the top of the first. Which method changes its winner first?
